digest.top_line: MSKCC T1-2N1 post-mastectomy: 10-yr LRR 7.0% without vs 4.0% with PMRT, but age <40 + LVI reached 28% without PMRT.
digest.tldr: A breast-only day on locoregional risk after surgery. MSKCC T1-2N1 and MGH node-negative cohorts support omitting PMRT at low risk, with age, LVI, margin and size picking out who still fails. NSABP pooled data put mortality HR 5.85 on oLRR. SAKK 23/82 TAM after RT for isolated LRR: 5y DFS 61% vs 40%, no OS gain.

sites.intro: Retrospective and pooled data dominate: these sharpen risk stratification for PMRT and regional RT, but none randomizes the RT decision itself.

studies.name: Locoregional recurrence after mastectomy in node-negative pts
studies.tldr: 10-yr LRR 6.0% in node-negative pts after mastectomy without PMRT, rising to 40.6% with 3 risk factors (>2cm, margin <2mm, premenopausal, LVI).
details: 🔍 Retrospective MGH cohort: 877 node-negative cases (870 pts), mastectomy + ALND, no PMRT, 1980-2000
🔍 T4 excluded. Median f/u 100 mo, median age 64, median 15 nodes examined
📊 10-yr cumulative incidence (CIF) of total LRR 6.0%, isolated LRR 4.3%
📊 Chest wall was the failure site in 80.4% of total LRR, 87.5% of isolated LRR

details.text: 📊 10-yr total LRR by univariate prognostic factor
📊 10-yr LRR by number of independent risk factors (size, margin, LVI, menopausal status)

details: 📐 MVA (Cox): size, margin, LVI, menopausal status independent; HRs ranged 2.6 to 3.8
📊 Grade on univariate only: 10-yr LRR 0% G1, 5.3% G2, 10% G3 (p=0.03)
⚠️ 3-factor estimate carries ±13.8%; only 1 pt had all 4 factors
⚠️ Systemic therapy in 276/877 only; pre-modern era likely inflates LRR vs current practice
⚠️ LVI not recorded was pooled with LVI absent, risking misclassification
⚠️ No PMRT arm: benefit is inferred from risk level, not measured

verdict.rationale: Single-institution retrospective risk model, no PMRT comparator; PMRT benefit inferred by analogy to node-positive trials. Sparse 3-factor subgroup, mostly no systemic therapy.
verdict.audience: Node-negative breast cancer, T1-T3, post-mastectomy + ALND, no PMRT

studies.significance: Chest wall carried 80.4% of failures, so the authors' case for chest-wall-only fields in selected pN0 pts rests on pattern-of-failure data, not just risk level. Margin <2mm (close 22%, positive 21% at 10 yr) is the factor most directly actionable at PMRT consult, ahead of the 3-factor 40.6% estimate with its ±13.8% error.
studies.monday_clinic: In a node-negative pt after mastectomy with a close or positive deep margin plus T2+ size or LVI, this supports raising chest-wall PMRT; it does not extend to pN0 pts with no adverse features (10-yr LRR 1.2%).

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **Retrospective** single-institution cohort (MGH), 877 cases in 870 pts treated 1980-2000. LRR estimated by cumulative incidence; Cox stepwise MVA. Median follow-up **100 mo**.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: **Node-negative** invasive breast cancer after mastectomy + axillary dissection, **no PMRT**; T4 excluded. Median age 64; 601 cases received no systemic therapy.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Total LRR** (first event, with or without simultaneous distant mets) and **isolated LRR** (no distant mets for ≥4 months). Only CIF results reported.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: 10-yr total LRR **6.0%**. Independent factors: **size >2 cm, margin <2 mm, premenopausal status, LVI**, with LRR climbing to **40.6%** with 3 factors.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: The IBCSG analysis of 1,275 node-negative women found size, LVI and menopausal status predictive but could not test margins (positive margins excluded). The authors anchor their threshold to the randomized PMRT trials, where node-positive and T3 pts with LRR approaching 30% gained a **9% absolute** survival benefit.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents node-negative pts after mastectomy with ALND and mostly no adjuvant systemic therapy. Does not represent pts on modern systemic therapy, sentinel-node-staged pts, or T4 disease.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: LVI not recorded was pooled with LVI absent. The higher LRR with chemo + hormones (12.6%) likely reflects selection, which the authors acknowledge, so systemic-therapy effects cannot be read from this series.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: Authors suggest **considering PMRT** for postmenopausal pts with all 3 of T2+, close/positive margin and LVI, or premenopausal pts with any 2. Because the chest wall dominates failure, **chest wall alone** without regional nodes may limit toxicity.

studies.interpretation:
The argument here is an extrapolation, and it should be read as one. The randomized PMRT trials established a survival benefit in node-positive and T3 disease where LRR approached 30%, and the authors reason that any node-negative subset with a comparable LRR risk should be treated as if it would see a comparable benefit. That chain has two links, and this paper supplies only the first: an estimate of LRR risk in pN0 pts by clinicopathologic factor. Whether RT delivers the same proportional reduction, and whether LRR reduction in a low-distant-risk pN0 population translates into survival the way it did in node-positive cohorts, is assumed rather than shown.

The risk stratification itself is more convincing in its broad shape than in its tail. The four independent factors line up with what the IBCSG node-negative analysis found for size, LVI and menopausal status, and this series adds margin status, which IBCSG could not assess because positive margins were excluded from its trials. Concordance across two independent datasets is the strongest thing the paper has. The headline 40.6% for three factors is the weakest: its standard error of 13.8% reflects a small subgroup, and only one patient carried all four. A reader quoting that number at a consult should hold it loosely; the step from 1.2% with no factors to 10.0% with one is the more stable signal.

The era cuts in a predictable direction. Most cases received no systemic therapy, and the authors state plainly that contemporary adjuvant therapy may lower LRR, so these absolute risks are probably ceilings for a modern patient. The paradoxical 12.6% LRR with combined chemo and hormones is best understood as confounding by indication, as the authors themselves say. Pooling LVI-not-recorded with LVI-absent may also have diluted the LVI contrast, which would bias the LVI effect toward the null rather than inflate it.

The pattern-of-failure data carry more practical weight than the risk score. With the chest wall accounting for 80.4% of total failures, the proposal to treat the chest wall without regional nodes in selected high-risk pN0 pts has a coherent rationale, and it is the piece most relevant to field design. It remains a hypothesis: no patient here received RT, so in-field control was never measured.

What would make this wrong: if modern systemic therapy compresses the high-risk tail well below the node-positive thresholds that justified PMRT, or if the margin effect reflects surgical-era practice that no longer applies. The paper is best used as a framework for weighing PMRT in a pN0 patient carrying several adverse features, rather than as evidence that RT improves outcomes in that patient.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Chest wall carried 80.4% of failures, supporting chest-wall-only fields if PMRT is offered to selected pN0 pts. Margin <2mm (close 22%, positive 21% at 10 yr) is the most actionable single factor, more reliable than the 3-factor 40.6% estimate with its ±13.8% error.

open_questions: Does PMRT reduce LRR or improve survival in multi-factor high-risk pN0 pts?
Do these LRR risks hold with modern systemic therapy?
Is chest-wall-only RT sufficient for high-risk pN0 pts?

studies.name: EBCTCG 20-year recurrence after stopping endocrine therapy at 5 years
studies.tldr: Distant recurrence 5-20y after stopping 5y ET ranged 13% (T1N0) to 41% (T2N4-9), with steady annual risk throughout, in ER+ early breast.
details: 🔍 IPD meta-analysis, 88 EBCTCG trials, 62,923 ER+ women disease-free at 5y after scheduled 5y ET
🔍 T1-T2, 0-9 positive nodes, age <75 at diagnosis; all had lymph-node dissection
💊 Assigned ET: 63% tamoxifen, 17% AI, 20% tamoxifen-AI sequence

details.text: 📊 Distant recurrence, years 5-20, by TN status
📊 T1N0 risk, years 5-20, by tumor grade
📊 20y risk from year 0 (n=74,194), by nodal status

details: 📊 T1N0 annual distant recurrence ~1% per year throughout years 5-20
📊 Contralateral BC ~0.3%/yr after stopping, independent of age or TN status
📐 Given TN status, grade and Ki-67 only moderately prognostic after year 5; PR and HER2 status not predictive
⚠️ ~50% diagnosed before 2000 (range 1976-2011); modern staging and therapy likely lower absolute risks
⚠️ Scheduled, not completed, 5y ET; authors estimate 5-10% of distant recurrences missed in trial records
⚠️ No gene-expression data; only 2% scheduled trastuzumab
⚠️ Locoregional recurrence followed the same risk factors as distant, but no LRR magnitudes reported in source text

verdict.rationale: Large IPD prognostic meta-analysis with long follow-up; quantifies recognized late-recurrence risk rather than testing an intervention. Older cohort, no genomic stratification.
verdict.audience: ER+ T1-2 N0-3 breast, disease-free after 5y adjuvant ET

studies.monday_clinic: In ER+ T1-T2 breast cancer with 0-9 nodes, disease-free after 5y of endocrine therapy, this supports TN-stage-based counselling on extending therapy, since even T1N0 low-grade disease carries 10% distant risk to year 20; it does not address genomically low-risk tumors or HER2+ disease treated with trastuzumab.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Individual-patient-data meta-analysis of **88 randomized trials** in the EBCTCG database; Kaplan-Meier and Cox regression stratified by trial and treatment. Analyses from year 5 to year 20.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: **62,923 women with ER+ T1-T2 disease, 0-9 positive nodes**, age <75, scheduled for 5y ET then stop, and event-free at year 5. Grade known in 43,590, Ki-67 in 7692; ~three quarters of node-positive pts had chemotherapy.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Main outcomes:** distant recurrence, any breast-cancer event (distant, locoregional, contralateral), and breast-cancer death by log-rank subtraction.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: Recurrences occurred at a **steady rate from year 5 to 20** in every TN category. Original **nodal status and tumor diameter** stayed the dominant determinants, with risks ranging **10% to 41%** by TN status and grade.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Earlier EBCTCG overviews established that 5y tamoxifen cuts recurrence ~50% during treatment and ~30% in the next 5 years. This analysis supplies the untreated-beyond-5y baseline against which extended-therapy trials such as ATLAS and MA.17 have to be read.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents ER+ T1-T2, 0-9 node pts disease-free after 5y scheduled ET, largely diagnosed before 2000. Does not represent ≥10 nodes, tumors >5 cm, age ≥75, or trastuzumab-treated HER2+ disease.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Grade and Ki-67 were often local reads. Chemotherapy effect after year 5 could not be assessed because receipt tracked nodal status, size and grade; no gene-expression profiles to identify a truly very-low-risk group.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: Even **T1N0 disease carried 13% distant risk** over years 5-20, so no TN subgroup was low enough to rule out benefit from extension. The absolute gain from extending ET scales with TN-stage baseline risk; the trade-off against fracture, thromboembolism and endometrial cancer remains to be settled by trial meta-analyses.

studies.interpretation:
The value of this paper is that it converts a well-known qualitative fact, late recurrence in ER-positive disease, into an absolute baseline that a clinician can multiply by a proportional benefit. The authors' logic is explicit: if extended endocrine therapy delivers roughly similar proportional reductions across risk groups, then the absolute gain from extension depends almost entirely on the risk a woman carries if she stops. That is what this analysis provides, stratified by the one variable that every clinic has for every patient, the original TN stage.

The most consequential finding is the shape, not any single number. Recurrence risk did not decay after year 5; it accrued at a roughly constant annual rate through year 20 in every TN stratum. That undercuts the intuition that a patient who reaches five clean years has passed the dangerous window. It also explains why the 20-year breast-cancer death figures from year 0 (15%, 28% and 49% for N0, N1-3 and N4-9) sit close behind distant recurrence: once past year 5, death tracks recurrence with only a short lag.

The second finding is that biology loses discriminating power after year 5 while anatomy keeps it. Grade and Ki-67 were strong early prognostic factors but only moderately informative later once TN status was known, and PR and HER2 status lost relevance entirely. This fits a model in which late recurrence reflects dormant disease burden seeded at diagnosis rather than proliferative tempo. It also tempers the hope that a single proliferation marker could identify women safe to stop; the authors searched for that low-risk subgroup and did not find one, with T1N0 low-grade tumors still carrying 10% distant risk.

Confidence should be adjusted in two directions. The cohort is old, roughly half diagnosed before 2000, with all women undergoing nodal dissection and few receiving trastuzumab, so modern staging migration and better systemic therapy probably push absolute risks down. Against that, the analysis counts scheduled rather than completed therapy, which inflates risk, while unrecorded recurrences, estimated at 5-10%, deflate it. The authors argue these roughly offset, which is plausible but unverifiable. The absence of gene-expression data is the larger gap, since a genomic score is now how many node-negative women are risk-stratified.

For radiation oncologists the paper is context rather than a decision tool: locoregional recurrence followed the same TN dependence, but no RT-specific magnitudes are reported. Its main use is in the medical oncology conversation about extending endocrine therapy, where it supplies the denominator against which toxicity must be weighed.

significance_by_specialty.medonc: Grade and Ki-67 lose most of their prognostic weight after year 5 once TN status is known, so original stage, not proliferation markers, should anchor the extension discussion. Even T1N0 low-grade disease carries 10% distant risk to year 20, leaving no TN subgroup where extension is clearly futile.

open_questions: Do genomic assays identify a truly low late-recurrence group?
Absolute benefit of extended ET versus fracture and thromboembolic risk
Late recurrence risk in modern-era, sentinel-node-staged cohorts

studies.name: SAKK 23/82
studies.tldr: Mature 11.6-yr f/u: 5y DFS 61% vs 40% with TAM after excision + RT for isolated post-mastectomy LRR; OS unchanged (median 11.5 vs 11.2 y, P=0.79).
details: 🔍 Phase III randomized, 178 randomized, 167 eligible; median f/u 11.6 yrs for surviving pts

details.text: 🔍 'Good risk' isolated locoregional recurrence (ILRR) after mastectomy
subdetails: ER+ recurrence, OR unknown ER with DFI >12 mo and <4 nodules, max diameter 3 cm
Sites: ipsilateral chest wall, shoulder, neck, upper arm, or regional nodes

details: 💊 After local Rx: TAM 20 mg/d until progression vs observation; stratified by menopausal status, adjuvant chemo, axillary nodes
🔍 Local Rx both arms: radical excision + RT 5000 cGy at 200 cGy/fx to involved region
📊 Of failure types, only further local recurrence was significantly reduced by TAM
⚠️ DFS gain borderline on log-rank (P=0.053); stronger P relies on early-weighted Gehan-Wilcoxon test
⚠️ Premenopausal subgroup small (n=35); OS deficit with TAM not statistically significant
⚠️ TAM-naive population; most modern ILRR pts have already had adjuvant endocrine therapy
🔗 Authors cite aromatase inhibitor activity in TAM-pretreated disease and IBCSG 27 (chemo vs local Rx alone) as the open follow-on

verdict.rationale: Randomized phase III with mature follow-up, but N=167, log-rank DFS P=0.053, no OS effect, and a TAM-naive pre-AI era population.
verdict.audience: ER+ or good-risk isolated LRR after mastectomy, post excision + RT, TAM-naive

studies.significance: The RT-relevant read is in-field durability: after excision plus 5000 cGy at 200 cGy/fx, further local recurrence was the only failure type TAM significantly reduced, while distant failure did not differ. Even without systemic therapy, 30% stayed free of further local and distant relapse, which supports treating ILRR with curative-intent local therapy.
studies.monday_clinic: In a postmenopausal woman with good-risk isolated post-mastectomy recurrence after excision and RT, this supports adding endocrine therapy for DFS; it does not extend to premenopausal pts, where 5y DFS was 60% either way, or to pts already exposed to adjuvant TAM.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Phase III randomized trial, accrual 1982 to 1991, central telephone randomization by SAKK. **178 randomized, 167 eligible** (11 ineligible). Mature analysis at **median 11.6 yrs** for surviving pts.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: **'Good risk' ILRR after mastectomy**: ER+ recurrence, or unknown ER with **DFI >12 mo and <4 nodules ≤3 cm**. Chest wall, shoulder, neck, upper arm or regional nodal recurrence. **Prior adjuvant TAM excluded.**

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Both arms: radical excision then RT to the recurrence site, **5000 cGy at 200 cGy/fx**, 5 days/week, to the involved region.

analysis_sections.label: Regimen
analysis_sections.body: **TAM 20 mg/d orally until progression** vs observation. Stratified by menopausal status, adjuvant chemo and axillary nodal involvement at diagnosis.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: DFS (events: local or distant recurrence, second malignancy, death) and OS, from randomization. Competing-risk cumulative incidence by first-failure site.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: DFS benefit persists at maturity (arm table above). Only **further local recurrence** was significantly reduced by TAM. The benefit was **confined to postmenopausal pts** (5y DFS 61% vs 33%, P=0.006).

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: No deaths from pulmonary embolism or endometrial cancer attributable to TAM in either menopausal group.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Authors describe this as the only randomized systemic-therapy ILRR trial to reach its accrual goal. They cite AI activity in TAM-pretreated metastatic disease and **IBCSG 27** (chemo vs local Rx alone) as the questions this trial leaves open.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents endocrine-naive, good-risk isolated post-mastectomy LRR fully excised and irradiated. Does not represent pts with prior adjuvant TAM, premenopausal pts, or poor-risk ILRR.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Strong DFS P (0.008) comes from the early-weighted Gehan-Wilcoxon test; log-rank is 0.053. Premenopausal OS signal (90% vs 67%) rests on n=35 and is unexplained.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: A durable DFS gain without OS benefit, driven by local rather than distant control. It challenges the view that ILRR is only a marker of inevitable metastasis, since about 40% achieve long-term disease freedom with local Rx plus TAM.

studies.interpretation:
The core message of SAKK 23/82 is less about tamoxifen than about what isolated locoregional recurrence after mastectomy actually is. The prevailing view when it was designed treated ILRR as a herald of distant disease, which made aggressive local therapy look futile. This trial's control arm argues otherwise for a selected population: after radical excision and 5000 cGy to the recurrence site, 30% of pts stayed free of further local and distant relapse without any systemic therapy, and about 40% did so with tamoxifen. The authors tie this to Fortin's observation that distant metastases peak later after ILRR than without it, suggesting the recurrence can itself seed metastasis and so deserves curative-intent eradication. For a radiation oncologist, that is the durable lesson: the local treatment in both arms is doing real work.

The tamoxifen effect deserves more caution than the 5y DFS gap of 61% vs 40% suggests. The log-rank P was 0.053; the 0.008 comes from Gehan-Wilcoxon, which weights early events. That pattern fits a benefit that delays relapse rather than preventing it, and it squares with the absence of any OS difference (median 11.5 vs 11.2 y). The failure-site analysis sharpens this: TAM significantly reduced only further local recurrence, not distant failure. Read through an RT lens, endocrine therapy here acts largely as an in-field and regional adjunct to excision and irradiation, so it is complementary to local therapy rather than a substitute for systemic control.

The menopausal split is where interpretation gets hardest. The DFS benefit sat entirely in postmenopausal pts (61% vs 33%, P=0.006), with premenopausal 5y DFS at 60% in both arms. The premenopausal OS finding, 90% with observation vs 67% with TAM, is provocative but based on 35 pts and P=0.175; the authors found no TAM toxicity to explain it and speculate about a trophic estrogen effect. This is a hypothesis to note, not a reason to withhold endocrine therapy from a young woman with an ER+ recurrence, especially as modern premenopausal endocrine strategies differ from TAM monotherapy.

Transfer to current practice is the main limit. Eligibility excluded prior adjuvant TAM, and almost every ER+ pt with an ILRR today has already received adjuvant endocrine therapy, often an aromatase inhibitor. The trial therefore answers a question that rarely arises in its original form. What carries forward is the principle that endocrine therapy after complete local treatment of an ER+ isolated recurrence improves DFS, which the authors extend by citing AI activity in TAM-pretreated disease. The chemotherapy question for poor-risk ILRR was left to IBCSG 27. Selection also matters: 'good risk' meant ER positivity or long DFI with small-volume disease, so the favorable control-arm outcomes should not be assumed for bulky, short-interval or receptor-negative recurrences.

What would make this wrong? A larger trial showing the DFS gain vanishes on a proportional-hazards analysis, or that the local-only benefit is fully replicated by modern RT technique alone. Neither exists, and with N=167 this remains the single randomized anchor for endocrine therapy after ILRR.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Excision plus 5000 cGy at 200 cGy/fx left 30% free of further relapse without systemic therapy, supporting curative-intent local treatment of ILRR. TAM's added benefit fell mainly on further local recurrence, not distant failure, so it complements rather than replaces in-field control.
significance_by_specialty.medonc: Endocrine therapy after complete local treatment of isolated LRR improved 5y DFS (61% vs 40%) with no OS gain, and only in postmenopausal pts (61% vs 33%, P=0.006). Population was TAM-naive, so transfer to today's endocrine-pretreated recurrences relies on authors' AI rationale, not this trial.

open_questions: Endocrine benefit after ILRR in pts with prior adjuvant TAM or AI
Role of chemotherapy for poor-risk ILRR
Why premenopausal pts derived no DFS benefit from TAM

studies.name: NSABP node-positive trials: prognosis after IBTR and locoregional recurrence
studies.tldr: Mortality HR 2.58 after IBTR and 5.85 after oLRR in node-positive pts treated with lumpectomy + WBI + chemo; 5y OS 59.9% vs 24.1%.
details: 🔍 Pooled analysis of the lumpectomy subset from five randomized NSABP node-positive trials (B-15, B-16, B-18, B-22, B-25)
🔍 N=2,669 node-positive pts treated with lumpectomy, WBI and adjuvant systemic therapy. Median time on study 13.3 yr
🔍 Negative margins were required for eligibility
📊 Locoregional failure in 424 (15.9%): IBTR 259 (9.7%), oLRR 165 (6.2%)

details.text: 📊 Outcomes after locoregional failure, IBTR vs oLRR
📊 Cumulative IBTR and oLRR incidence by protocol (Table 3)
📊 5-yr DDFS 12.1% (95% CI 5.6-26.4%) after supraclavicular recurrence vs 31.5% (19.9-49.7%) after axillary recurrence

details: 📊 IBTR was not associated with nodal count (P=.53)

details.text: 📊 Pathologic tumor >4 cm vs ≤2 cm: 10-yr IBTR 14.3% vs 7.5% (P=.045)

details: 📊 Later IBTR carried a >40% reduction in 3-yr mortality risk vs earlier IBTR, across cutoffs
📊 3-yr OS only 15.3% when oLRR occurred within 2 yr of the primary
⚠️ Recurrence was not a randomized exposure. HRs are prognostic, not the survival gain better local control would recover
⚠️ WBI dose, boost and regional nodal fields not stated in source
⚠️ Premenopausal women got no tamoxifen regardless of ER, which confounds the age signal for IBTR
⚠️ IBTR not split into true recurrence vs new ipsilateral primary

verdict.rationale: Pooled secondary analysis of five randomized NSABP trials; recurrence is a non-randomized prognostic exposure. Consistent with prior IBTR prognosis series the authors cite.
verdict.audience: Node-positive breast, lumpectomy + WBI + adjuvant chemo, negative margins

studies.significance: Supraclavicular failures were the largest oLRR group (81 of 165) and carried 5y DDFS 12.1% vs 31.5% after axillary recurrence. 10y oLRR reached 14.6% with ≥10 positive nodes. Regional nodal RT use is not stated in source, so this is the natural-history case for nodal coverage in node-positive BCS, not a test of it.
studies.monday_clinic: For node-positive pts treated with lumpectomy, WBI and chemo who then develop isolated IBTR or oLRR, this supports counseling the recurrence as a marker of high distant and mortality risk rather than a purely local event; it does not address whether upfront regional nodal RT prevents it.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **Pooled secondary analysis** of the lumpectomy subset from five randomized NSABP node-positive trials. IBTR and oLRR were modeled as **time-varying covariates** in Cox models for OS and distant disease.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: 10,010 women entered; **2,669 node-positive pts after lumpectomy** were eligible, median time on study 13.3 yr. **Negative margins required**. About two thirds had 1-3 involved nodes.

analysis_sections.label: Regimen
analysis_sections.body: AC, CMF and tamoxifen-based arms. B-22 and B-25 tested cyclophosphamide intensification. **Premenopausal women received no tamoxifen** irrespective of ER.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Whole-breast irradiation after lumpectomy. **Dose, fractionation, boost and regional nodal fields not stated in source.**

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: IBTR tracked **age, tumor size and ER**; oLRR tracked **nodal burden and ER/PgR**. Effect sizes are in the table above.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Extends earlier NSABP and single-institution IBTR prognosis series (Fisher, Haffty, Whelan) to chemotherapy-treated node-positive disease. Its supraclavicular-dominant oLRR pattern is the biology later tested in regional nodal RT trials such as MA.20 and EORTC 22922.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents node-positive pts treated with lumpectomy, WBI and anthracycline/CMF-era chemo with negative margins. Does not represent mastectomy pts, node-negative disease, or HER2-directed and taxane-era therapy.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Accrual 1984-1994, ER by fmol, **no HER2 or subtype data**. Subsite DDFS estimates rest on small numbers with wide CIs. Multivariable models used the 2,416 pts with complete covariates.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: A locoregional failure in this population is **mostly a systemic-risk event**, oLRR far more than IBTR. The paper cannot say whether preventing the failure would change survival, or whether the nodal failures arose in treated or untreated volumes.

studies.interpretation:
The central message is that in node-positive disease treated with lumpectomy, whole-breast irradiation and adjuvant chemotherapy, a locoregional failure is rarely only local. IBTR carried a mortality HR of 2.58 and oLRR 5.85, with adjustment for age, nodal count, tumor size and ER. The modeling choice matters more than the headline numbers. Treating recurrence as a time-varying covariate avoids the immortal-time trap of comparing pts who recurred with everyone else from baseline, which is how many earlier single-institution series built their case. That makes these hazards more credible than most of the literature the authors cite. It does not make them causal. Recurrence was not randomized, and the excess hazard cannot be read as the survival that better local control would recover, because a recurrence may simply flag biology that was going to metastasize anyway.

For a radiation oncologist the useful part is the split between IBTR and oLRR. oLRR was dominated by supraclavicular failures (81 of 165), and those pts had 5y DDFS of 12.1% against 31.5% after axillary recurrence, though both intervals are wide. Unlike IBTR, oLRR tracked nodal burden, with 10y incidence of 4.4% for 1-3 nodes and 14.6% for ≥10. That gradient reads as regional disease biology rather than inadequate breast treatment, and it is the rationale later tested in regional nodal irradiation trials such as MA.20 and EORTC 22922. The source does not describe nodal fields, so one cannot tell whether these failures arose in untreated or undertreated volumes. This paper motivates the nodal question; it cannot answer it.

The IBTR signal needs more care. Later IBTR was associated with more than a 40% reduction in 3-yr mortality risk compared with earlier IBTR, and the authors suggest late events include second ipsilateral primaries. Because true recurrences and new primaries were not separated, the pooled IBTR hazard averages two different entities, and the hazard for true recurrence is probably understated. The age gradient for IBTR (10y 11.1% under 50 vs 5.1% at 60 or older) is confounded by protocol design, since premenopausal women received no tamoxifen regardless of ER. Some of the young-age risk may therefore be untreated ER-positive disease rather than age itself.

Transfer to current practice is limited by era. Accrual ran from 1984 to 1994: anthracycline and CMF backbones, no taxanes, no HER2 testing or HER2-directed therapy, ER measured in fmol, and no endocrine therapy for premenopausal women. Absolute locoregional failure rates today are lower, and the post-recurrence survival figures here should not be quoted to a contemporary patient. The relative message, that oLRR carries a much worse prognosis than IBTR and that both signal distant risk, is more likely to hold. What would undercut it is a model including molecular subtype. If recurrence is mostly a surrogate for subtype biology, the independent hazard attached to the event would shrink once subtype is accounted for. The authors also note that systemic therapy at isolated recurrence had not been tested in randomized trials at the time, so the paper leaves that management question open.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Supraclavicular sites made up 81 of 165 oLRRs, with 5y DDFS 12.1% after supraclavicular recurrence. 10y oLRR reached 14.6% with ≥10 nodes. Nodal RT fields are not stated in source, so this is natural-history support for regional coverage in node-positive BCS, not evidence that it prevents these failures.
significance_by_specialty.medonc: Mortality HR 5.85 and adjusted distant-disease HR 6.68 after oLRR frame isolated locoregional failure as systemic-risk disease. The source notes chemotherapy at recurrence was untested in randomized trials. The AC/CMF backbone with no taxane or HER2 therapy limits how far the magnitudes transfer.

Does true recurrence vs new ipsilateral primary change prognosis after IBTR?

studies.name: T1-2N1 mastectomy without PMRT (MSKCC)
studies.tldr: 10-yr LRR 7.0% without vs 4.0% with PMRT in T1-2N1 after mastectomy; age <40 + LVI reached 28% without PMRT.
details: 🔍 Retrospective single-institution (MSKCC prospective database), mastectomy 1995-2006, N=1087
🔍 PMRT at physician discretion: 163 (15%) PMRT vs 924 (85%) no PMRT
🔍 Excluded T3/T4, NAC, and isolated tumor cells only
🔍 ALND in 94.2%, median 18 nodes resected; median f/u 10.8 yr

details.text: 📊 PMRT vs no PMRT, 10-yr outcomes (unadjusted, non-randomized)
📊 No-PMRT group: LRR by age and LVI (Fig 2)

details: 📐 MVA for LRR without PMRT: age <40 HR 4.15 (95% CI 2.42-7.11), LVI HR 3.47 (95% CI 1.92-6.29)
🔍 PMRT fields: chest wall in all; SCV 137/163 (84%), axilla 7 (4%), IMN 6 (4%); dose not reported
🔗 vs EBCTCG 1-3 node subset: LRR 20.3 → 3.8% at 10 yr with PMRT, from 1965-1986 era trials
⚠️ PMRT arm enriched for ECE, LVI, 3 nodes, macrometastases; arm comparison is confounded by indication
⚠️ <40 + LVI subgroup: 28% printed with 95% CI 11.0-22.1, which does not contain the estimate
⚠️ Authors state omission does not apply to 1-3 positive sentinel nodes without completion ALND

verdict.rationale: Retrospective single-institution series; PMRT assigned by physician to higher-risk pts, so the null arm comparison cannot support omission. Valid mainly as an untreated-LRR baseline.
verdict.audience: T1-2N1 breast, mastectomy + ALND, adjuvant systemic, no NAC

studies.significance: The no-PMRT baseline only holds after full ALND (median 18 nodes): 10-yr LRR 2% at age ≥40 without LVI vs 28% at <40 with LVI. Failures clustered at chest wall (51%) and supraclavicular nodes (27%), so where PMRT is used here, the target is chest wall plus SCV. The axilla is not.
studies.monday_clinic: In a woman ≥40 without LVI after mastectomy plus ALND for T1-2N1 disease, this supports discussing PMRT omission (10-yr LRR 2% untreated). It does not extend to SLNB-only axillae or to pts <40 with LVI.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Retrospective review of the MSKCC prospectively maintained database, mastectomy **1995-2006**, **N=1087**. PMRT given at physician discretion. Median follow-up **10.8 yr**.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: **T1-2 with 1-3 positive LNs**; excluded T3/T4, NAC and isolated tumor cells. ALND in **94.2%** (median 18 nodes), chemotherapy in 88%, all ER+ pts received endocrine therapy.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: All PMRT pts received chest-wall RT. SCV in **137/163 (84%)**, axilla in 7 (4%), IMN in 6 (4%). Dose and fractionation not reported.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Primary:** LRR, RFS and OS, by Kaplan-Meier and Cox regression. Predictors of LRR modeled in the no-PMRT group.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: Arm comparison was null for all three endpoints (table). In the no-PMRT group, **age <40 (HR 4.15)** and **LVI (HR 3.47)** were the only independent LRR predictors.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Untreated LRR of **7.0%** sits far below the **20.3%** in the EBCTCG 1-3 node subset, whose trials used CMF-era chemo and limited axillary clearance. EORTC 22922 reported a death HR of **0.91** in its mastectomy subgroup, which the authors argue weakens its application here.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents T1-2N1 pts after mastectomy with completion ALND and modern adjuvant systemic therapy. Does not represent SLNB-only axillae, post-NAC pts, or T3/T4 disease.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Pre-2006 cohort with only 41% of HER2-amplified pts receiving trastuzumab. The 28% subgroup estimate carries a printed CI (11.0-22.1) that excludes it, and pathology slides were not re-reviewed.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The useful output is risk stratification of the untreated population, not the PMRT vs no-PMRT comparison. It **does not settle** omission in the post-Z0011/AMAROS era of axillary de-escalation.

studies.interpretation:
The paper's title claims more than its design can deliver. The PMRT and no-PMRT groups were not comparable: physicians selected the 15% who got radiation because they were younger and had more nodes, extracapsular extension, LVI and macrometastases. That the two groups had similar 10-year LRR, RFS and OS says only that PMRT brought a high-risk group roughly level with a low-risk one. It does not say PMRT adds nothing, and the authors themselves warn against reading Fig 1 as if it came from a randomized comparison. The defensible output is narrower and still useful: a well-followed estimate of untreated locoregional risk in a modern-systemic-therapy T1-2N1 population, and a split of that risk by two easily measured features.

That split carries the clinical value. Age under 40 and LVI separate a 2% 10-year LRR from a 28% one. At the low end, the absolute PMRT benefit would have to come from a tiny base, and the toxicity side of the ledger (lymphedema, cardiac dose, reconstruction complications) dominates. At the high end, untreated risk is in the range where the EBCTCG data showed the LRR reduction translating into a breast cancer mortality benefit. One caution: the 28% figure is printed with a 95% CI of 11.0-22.1, which cannot be right. Either the estimate or the interval is a transcription error, and a reader should treat the high-risk cell as directionally strong but numerically uncertain, resting on 75 pts at baseline.

The gap between this series and the EBCTCG 1-3 node subset (20.3% untreated LRR) is the central argument for de-escalation, and the authors attribute it to anthracycline/taxane chemotherapy, aromatase inhibitors and thorough axillary clearance. The last factor is the one that dates the paper. With 94.2% undergoing ALND and a median of 18 nodes removed, these pts were fully staged and surgically cleared. Practice has since moved toward leaving positive sentinel nodes in place, and the authors explicitly state their omission argument does not cover that population. A radiation oncologist seeing a sentinel-node-only N1 mastectomy patient cannot borrow these LRR estimates, because the residual nodal burden is different and unmeasured.

The pattern of failure points to a technique question that the subgroup analysis does not answer. Chest wall and supraclavicular recurrences made up most events, and only 10 of 63 involved the axilla, consistent with a dissected axilla. Where PMRT is chosen for a high-risk phenotype after ALND, this supports chest wall plus supraclavicular coverage rather than full-axilla fields. IMN failures were rare, but IMN was treated in only 6 pts, so the series is uninformative on IMN coverage.

What would make the conclusion wrong: unmeasured selection (pts deemed low-risk for reasons not captured, such as comorbidity limiting follow-up), incomplete LRR capture outside MSKCC, and a HER2 cohort largely untreated with trastuzumab, which cuts in both directions for applicability. The randomized test of this exact population is SUPREMO. This series should be read as a risk-stratification companion to that kind of evidence, not as a substitute for it.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Untreated LRR splits by age and LVI, from 2% (≥40, no LVI) to 28% (<40, LVI) at 10 yr. Recurrences were chest wall 51% and supraclavicular 27%, axilla 8%. That supports chest wall plus SCV over axillary coverage when PMRT is given for this phenotype.
significance_by_specialty.surgonc: The low no-PMRT LRR depends on completion ALND: 94.2% had ALND, median 18 nodes. The authors exclude SLNB-only 1-3 positive nodes from the omission argument, so a surgeon skipping completion ALND can't use this series to justify also omitting PMRT.

Optimal nodal targets when PMRT is given for T1-2N1

papers.title: Adjuvant therapy after excision and radiation of isolated postmastectomy locoregional breast cancer recurrence: definitive results of a phase III randomized trial (SAKK 23/82) comparing tamoxifen with observation
Prognosis After Ipsilateral Breast Tumor Recurrence and Locoregional Recurrences in Five National Surgical Adjuvant Breast and Bowel Project Node-Positive Adjuvant Breast Cancer Trials
papers.abstract: Purpose Locoregional failure after breast-conserving surgery is associated with increased risk of distant disease and death. The magnitude of this risk in patients receiving chemotherapy has not been adequately characterized. Patients and Methods Our study population included 2,669 women randomly assigned onto five National Surgical Adjuvant Breast and Bowel Project node-positive protocols (B-15, B-16, B-18, B-22, and B-25), who were treated with lumpectomy, whole-breast irradiation, and adjuvant systemic therapy. Cumulative incidences of ipsilateral breast tumor recurrence (IBTR) and other locoregional recurrence (oLRR) were calculated. Kaplan-Meier curves were used to estimate distant–disease-free survival (DDFS) and overall survival (OS) after IBTR or oLRR. Cox models were used to model survival using clinical and pathologic factors jointly with IBTR or oLRR as time-varying predictors. Results Four hundred twenty-four patients (15.9%) experienced locoregional failure; 259 (9.7%) experienced IBTR, and 165 (6.2%) experienced oLRR. The 10-year cumulative incidence of IBTR and oLRR was 8.7% and 6.0%, respectively. Most locoregional failures occurred within 5 years (62.2% for IBTR and 80.6% for oLRR). Age, tumor size, and estrogen receptor status were significantly associated with IBTR. Nodal status and estrogen and progesterone receptor status were significantly associated with oLRR. The 5-year DDFS rates after IBTR and oLRR were 51.4% and 18.8%, respectively. The 5-year OS rates after IBTR and oLRR were 59.9% and 24.1%, respectively. Hazard ratios for mortality associated with IBTR and oLRR were 2.58 (95% CI, 2.11 to 3.15) and 5.85 (95% CI, 4.80 to 7.13), respectively. Conclusion Node-positive breast cancer patients who developed IBTR or oLRR had significantly poorer prognoses than patients who did not experience these events.
